subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Functional groups: classification of organic compounds
bigPicture: Organic chemistry is sorted by functional groups: the reactive part of the molecule that gives a family (homologous series) its typical properties. Learn the groups, the naming rules and the kinds of isomer, then (HL) use mass spectrometry, IR and ¹H NMR spectra together to work out an unknown structure.

keyIdeas.cue: Which types of formula are used?
keyIdeas.answer: Empirical (simplest ratio), molecular (actual atoms, C₄H₁₀), full structural (every bond), condensed (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃), skeletal (zig-zag lines, C and H on C not drawn) and stereochemical (wedges and dashes; only draw these when asked). Be able to convert between molecular, structural and skeletal; 3D models help.

keyIdeas.cue: Which functional groups must you know?
keyIdeas.answer: Halogeno –X; hydroxyl –OH; carbonyl C=O (aldehyde –CHO, ketone C–CO–C); carboxyl –COOH; alkoxy –OR (ethers); amino –NH₂; amido –CONH₂; ester –COO–; phenyl –C₆H₅. Saturated = only C–C single bonds; unsaturated = contains C=C or C≡C.

A family with the same functional group and general formula, where each member differs by CH₂: alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, halogenoalkanes, alcohols CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, ethers, amines, amides, esters. Members have similar chemical properties.

keyIdeas.cue: Why do boiling points rise along a series?
keyIdeas.answer: Each extra CH₂ adds electrons and surface area, so London forces get stronger and the boiling point rises steadily. Branching lowers the boiling point (less surface contact).

Find the longest chain containing the functional group (up to 6 C: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-). Number from the end that gives the functional group (or branch) the lowest number. Add substituent prefixes (methyl, chloro; di/tri for repeats) in alphabetical order. Suffixes: -ane, -ene, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid; halogens as prefixes. Examples: 2-methylbutane, but-2-ene, propan-2-ol, butanone, 2-chloropropane.

Same molecular formula, different connectivity. Chain (branched vs straight), position (functional group in a different place) and functional group isomers (propanal vs propanone). Primary/secondary/tertiary: the carbon bearing –OH or –X is bonded to 1, 2 or 3 other carbons; for amines, count the carbons on N.

Same connectivity, different spatial arrangement. Cis-trans isomerism: restricted rotation about C=C (or in a ring) with two different groups on each carbon; cis = same side. Optical isomerism: a chiral carbon has four different groups; the two enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions; a racemic mixture (50 : 50) is optically inactive. Enantiomers behave differently in chiral environments (e.g. drugs and enzymes). Draw with wedge-dash bonds.

keyIdeas.cue: How is mass spectrometry used for organic molecules (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: The molecular ion M⁺ (highest significant m/z) gives Mr. Fragment peaks come from bonds breaking: the difference from M tells you what was lost (15 = CH₃, 17 = OH, 29 = C₂H₅ or CHO, 45 = COOH; see booklet).

keyIdeas.cue: What does an IR spectrum tell you (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: Bonds absorb IR at characteristic wavenumbers (cm⁻¹). Key bands: broad O–H 3200–3600 (alcohol); very broad O–H 2500–3000 (carboxylic acid); C=O 1700–1750; C=C 1620–1680. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, H₂O, CH₄) absorb IR because their vibrations change the dipole.

keyIdeas.cue: What does ¹H NMR tell you (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: Number of signals = number of different hydrogen environments. Chemical shift (ppm, relative to TMS at 0) shows the type of environment (booklet table). Integration (relative peak areas) gives the ratio of H atoms in each environment.

n + 1 rule: a signal from H with n equivalent H on neighbouring carbons splits into n + 1 peaks: singlet (0 neighbours), doublet (1), triplet (2), quartet (3). Ethyl group = triplet (CH₃) + quartet (CH₂). OH usually appears as a singlet.
Use empirical formula and MS for the molecular formula; IR for functional groups; ¹H NMR for the carbon skeleton and environments. Check that the final structure fits every piece of data.

keyTerms.def: Atom or group that gives a series its characteristic reactions.
Family with the same functional group and general formula, differing by CH₂.
Carbon bonded to four different groups (AHL).
Position of an NMR signal (ppm) reflecting the H environment (AHL).
Relative area of NMR signals = ratio of H atoms (AHL).

workedExamples.title: Naming
steps: Longest chain with OH = 4 C, OH on C2 from the nearer end.
Second: longest chain 5 C, methyl on C3.

workedExamples.title: Combining spectra (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: C₃H₆O: IR strong band at 1715 cm⁻¹, no broad 3200–3600 band; ¹H NMR one singlet; MS M⁺ 58 and a large peak at 43.
steps: IR: C=O, no O–H → aldehyde or ketone.
One NMR signal → all H equivalent → propanone (CH₃COCH₃); propanal would give three signals.

misconceptions.wrong: Branched isomers have higher boiling points.
misconceptions.right: Branching reduces surface contact and London forces, so boiling points are lower.

misconceptions.wrong: Number of NMR peaks in a split cluster = number of H on that carbon.
misconceptions.right: Splitting depends on H on the neighbouring carbons (n + 1 rule).

misconceptions.wrong: A racemic mixture contains no chiral molecules.
misconceptions.right: It contains equal amounts of both enantiomers, so rotations cancel.

practice.prompt: Identify the functional groups in CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and H₂NCH₂COOH.
Draw and name the three structural isomers of C₅H₁₂.
Deduce the number of signals and their splitting in the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanoic acid.
checkpoints: Both singlets (no H on neighbouring C)

practice.prompt: Explain why butan-2-ol shows optical isomerism but propan-2-ol does not.
checkpoints: C2 in butan-2-ol has four different groups (H, OH, CH₃, C₂H₅): chiral
C2 in propan-2-ol has two CH₃ groups: not chiral

paper1A.stem: What is the name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO?
Which pair are functional group isomers?

paper1A.why: C–OH carbon bonded to three carbons.

paper1A.stem: How many signals are in the ¹H NMR spectrum of propan-2-ol?
paper1A.why: Two equivalent CH₃, one CH, one OH.

paper1A.stem: Which compound has a chiral carbon?
paper1A.why: C2 has H, Cl, CH₃, C₂H₅.

paper1B.data: Unknown X, C₂H₄O₂. IR: very broad 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ and strong 1710 cm⁻¹. ¹H NMR: singlet at 2.1 ppm (3H), singlet at 11.5 ppm (1H).
paper1B.prompt: Identify X, using the booklet IR and NMR tables.
paper1B.answer: Carboxylic acid O–H and C=O; NMR: CH₃ next to C=O and COOH proton (9.0–13.0 ppm). X is ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH.

assessmentNote: Paper 1A = multiple choice, no calculator; Paper 1B = data-based questions (format from public sources, confirm with the official guide). All prompts here are original practice, not predictions of exam questions.

errorHints.hint: Learn suffixes and which groups are prefixes (halogens, methyl).
In NMR, count environments first, then integration, then splitting from neighbours.
Match IR bands and NMR shifts to the booklet ranges, quoting the range used.
Show the full name with locants and hyphens/commas: 2,2-dimethylpropane.
